In early 1972, introduced by Lee Underwood, he played it live with Tim Buckley in southern California and gradually revised the instrument; the first production model appeared in 1974, and Chapman demonstrated it publicly the same year. Musicians such as Alphonso Johnson and Tony Levin took it up early, which brought the Chapman Stick into recording and touring; from 1981 Levin used it in the band, and after Trey Gunn joined in 1994 the two-Stick line-up took shape.

The Chapman Stick is an electric chordophone designed by the American Emmett Chapman in the early 1970s, and belongs to the guitar family. The body is like a lengthened and widened electric guitar fretboard, usually with 10 or 12 individually tuned strings, fitted with passive or active pickup modules and pluggable into an amplifier, and a special pickup can trigger synthesizers. The player taps the strings with the fingers of both hands on the frets or behind the fretboard to sound them, and can play bass, chords and melody at once. Musicians such as Emmett Chapman, Alphonso Johnson and Tony Levin have used it in live performance, recording and touring.
查普曼觸弦琴琴身材質隨年代改變：早期以硬木為主，多為鐵木，亦有烏木與其他異國木材: The material of the Chapman Stick body changed over the years: early ones were mainly hardwood, often ironwood, and also ebony and other exotic timbers; in the 1980s some were made of injection-moulded polycarbonate resin, later giving way to a one-piece hardwood structure with an adjustable steel reinforcement; from 2001 to the mid-2000s there were also structural graphite and continuous carbon-fibre models. Current bodies are made of laminated hardwood, laminated bamboo and graphite. The fretboard carries stainless steel pyramid-shaped frets; the materials of the sounding strings and the other parts are not recorded in the sources.
演奏查普曼觸弦琴時，可將琴掛在皮帶鉤與肩帶上，琴身約與垂直呈三十至四十度，讓雙手: To play the Chapman Stick, hang it from the belt hook and shoulder strap with the body at about 30 to 40 degrees from vertical, so that both hands reach the fretboard naturally; in a seated position a cross-member laid on the knees carries the belt hook. Sound comes from tapping the strings with the fingertips on the fretboard or near the tuning machines, much as one strikes a piano key, usually with one hand on the treble melody and the other on the bass rhythm. Begin with the classic tuning: bass strings in fifths and melody strings in fourths, lowest in the centre and highest at the edges, and practise the division of labour between the hands with a grand staff or a tablature system that gives the fingering.
